papers.title: Approach to some data preparation problems in systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: In systematic review, the measures reported by the primary studies may not always be the measures sought by the systematic review investigators. Motivated by an systematic review of interventions to reduce meat consumption, we discuss here methods to infer relative risks and confidence intervals from randomized controlled trials that reported differences, possibly in the presence of repeated measures or multiple interventions.

papers.title: Development and Validation of a Sleep Disorder Risk Prediction Model in Young and Middle-Aged Adults With Anemia
papers.abstract: Objective This study aimed to develop and validate a predictive model for sleep disorders in young and middle-aged adults with anemia, providing evidence for early identification, risk stratification, and individualized sleep management. Methods Data in the NHANES were analyzed and randomly divided into development and validation cohorts. LASSO regression was used to screen optimal predictors in the development cohort, followed by univariate and multivariate logistic regression to identify independent predictors and construct a nomogram. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curves, calibration curves, Brier scores, and decision curve analysis. Results The weighted prevalence of sleep disorders among young and middle-aged adults with anemia was 10.19%. Multivariate logistic regression identified seven independent predictors: sex, monocyte count, asthma, overweight, arthritis, congestive heart failure, and hypertension. The model showed good discrimination, with area under the curve values of 0.817 in the development cohort and 0.791 in the validation cohort. Calibration was satisfactory, with Brier scores of 0.074 and 0.075, respectively. Decision curve analysis indicated favorable clinical net benefit in both cohorts. Conclusion The proposed predictive model demonstrated good discrimination, calibration, and may help healthcare providers identify young and middle-aged adults with anemia who are at high risk for sleep disorders.

papers.title: Patterns and correlates of alcohol and other substance use among adults in two communities in Cape Town: a cross-sectional
papers.abstract: Background We aimed to characterize substance use patterns, and their correlates, among adults with and without HIV at two healthcare facilities in Cape Town, South Africa. Methods We recruited adults with and without HIV from two primary healthcare facilities. We assessed alcohol use with the AUDIT-C and other substance use with the WHO-ASSIST questionnaires. We classified participants with no lifetime drug use and no or low-risk alcohol use as "low risk" and fitted latent class models among remaining participants to identify additional substance use patterns. We used multinomial logistic regression to examine factors associated with substance use patterns. Results Among 602 participants, 265 (44.0%) were "low risk". Latent class analysis among the remaining 337 identified three patterns: "higher-risk alcohol use" (N=168; 27.9%), "cannabis use" (universal cannabis use with mixed alcohol risk; N=114; 18.9%), and "mixed illicit drug use" (predominantly no or low-risk alcohol use with use of multiple drugs; N=55; 9.1%). Participants younger than 45 years were less likely to be in the low-risk group. Male sex was associated with lower probability of the low-risk group and higher probability of the higher-risk alcohol use and cannabis use classes. HIV was associated with higher probability of higher-risk alcohol use. One facility had a substantially higher probability of mixed illicit drug use. Conclusions We identified distinct higher-risk substance use profiles that varied strongly by age, sex, and facility. These findings support integrating alcohol and substance use screening and management into primary care and tailoring responses to local substance use patterns.

papers.title: Visit-to-Visit Blood Pressure Variability, Glycemic Status and the Risk of Dementia, Stroke, and All-Cause Mortality: A UK Biobank Cohort Study
papers.abstract: Aims: The risks of dementia, stroke, and mortality increase from normoglycemia to prediabetes and type 2 diabetes (T2D). Blood pressure variability (BPV) is associated with adverse vascular and neurological outcomes, but its role in glycemia-associated risks remains unclear. We examined the interplay between glycemia, BPV, and these outcomes. Methods and Results: In a large prospective cohort, visit-to-visit BPV was quantified using absolute and directional measures of systolic (SBP), diastolic (DBP), mean arterial (MAP), and pulse pressure (PP). Glycemic status was defined as normoglycemia, prediabetes, and T2D. Time-updated Cox models estimated outcome associations, adjusting for confounders and mean blood pressure. We evaluated the joint and independent associations of BPV and glycemic status with outcomes, effect modification, and attenuation of glycemia-associated risks after BPV adjustment. Among 57,611 participants (median follow-up, 5.1 years; IQR, 3.3-9.5 years), compared with normoglycemia and low BPV, T2D with high SBP variability was associated with higher risks of all-cause mortality (HR 2.80, 95% CI 2.12-3.69) and nominally higher risk of all-cause dementia (HR 2.46, 95% CI 1.37-4.42). All absolute BPV measures were independently associated with mortality, while DBP and MAP variability were associated with overall stroke after FDR correction. Additional adjustment for BPV minimally attenuated glycemia-associated risk, and no multiplicative interaction remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Conclusions: Absolute BPV was associated with mortality, and DBP and MAP variability with overall stroke, after accounting for glycemic status and mean blood pressure. Additional BPV adjustment changed the glycemic association only minimally.

papers.title: Language eligibility criteria and enrolled racial and ethnic composition in US clinical trials: a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Federal policy now requires sponsors to submit diversity action plans for clinical trials, yet the modifiable features of trial design associated with enrolled composition remain poorly characterized. English-language proficiency requirements are written into eligibility criteria and recorded as free text in a public registry, making them visible and, in principle, amenable to revision, but their relationship to enrolled composition has been examined only within single disease areas and in small samples of trials. We examined whether these requirements and documented language accommodation were associated with the racial and ethnic composition of enrolled participants. METHODS AND FINDINGS: We conducted a cross-sectional study of interventional trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov with at least one US site and posted results, using a registry snapshot retrieved in October 2026. The primary cohort comprised the 44,487 trials with exclusively US sites, of which 21,924 (49.3%) reported baseline race and 17,434 (39.2%) reported baseline ethnicity with counts that reconciled with the posted denominator. Both exposures were classified from free-text eligibility criteria using regular expressions validated against independent physician review of 150 trials. For the English-language requirement classifier, sensitivity was 88.2% and specificity was 99.2%. The outcome was the trial-level proportion of enrolled participants in each category, analyzed using generalized linear models adjusted for intervention class, therapeutic area, sponsor, phase, enrollment, sites, start year, US Census region, and the population composition of the trial's site states. An English-language proficiency requirement appeared in 5,736 trials (12.9%); its prevalence rose from 7.4% of trials starting in 2010 to 26.2% in 2023 (odds ratio [OR] per decade 2.91, P<0.001), whereas documented accommodation, an eligibility statement allowing participation in a language other than English (Spanish in 99.9% of flagged trials), remained rare (788 trials, 1.8%). The requirement was associated with lower enrolled proportions of Asian (OR=0.85, 95% CI 0.77-0.93, P=0.001) and Hispanic/Latinx participants (OR=0.85, 95% CI 0.79-0.91, P<0.001), with no evidence of an association for White participants (OR=0.99, 95% CI 0.95-1.04, P=0.75). Documented accommodation was associated with a higher proportion of Hispanic/Latinx participants (OR=3.23, 95% CI 2.82-3.71, P<0.001). Geographic adjustment did not change the statistical significance of the requirement associations and attenuated the accommodation association. The main limitations were the cross-sectional design, which precludes causal inference; the restriction of enrollment analyses to trials reporting baseline demographics, which were more recent than those without such reporting; and possible misclassification of automatically classified exposures. CONCLUSIONS: English-language proficiency requirements became more than three times as common between 2010 and 2023 and were associated with lower enrolled proportions of Asian and Hispanic/Latinx participants. Less common documented language accommodation was associated with a higher enrolled proportion of Hispanic/Latinx participants. Because these criteria are investigator-written and publicly recorded, they may be a tractable target for improving enrollment equity, although whether revising them changes who enrolls requires prospective evaluation

papers.title: Dynamics of a slow-burn epidemic: the genomic epidemiology of poultry-associated Campylobacter jejuni ST474 in New Zealand
papers.abstract: The emergence of a dominant poultry-associated strain of Campylobacter jejuni in New Zealand coincided with a multi-year epidemic of human campylobacteriosis. This was characterised by an increase in cases to 2006, when one of the highest national case-rates in the world was recorded, followed by a rapid decline attributed to interventions in the poultry industry. The strain belonged to an internationally rare multilocus sequence type, ST474 - a member of Clonal Complex (CC) 48 - that was highly prevalent in both poultry and human cases in New Zealand but was also identified in other samples. ST474 isolates from humans, animal reservoirs and environmental water samples were collected between 2005 and 2019 and whole genome sequenced (N=443). Isolates from a 2018/9 case-control study of campylobacteriosis in New Zealand were included for genomic comparisons with other sequence types and CCs. This presented an opportunity to examine the genomic epidemiology of a single, relatively recently emerged lineage of C. jejuni, and improve our understanding of drivers of emergence and persistence in a relatively isolated ecosystem. Six subpopulations (clades) of ST474 were identified and these varied in terms of their host association, persistence, patterns of homologous recombination, and complement of mobile genetic elements, including plasmids and chromosomally integrated elements. Clade E was associated with a single poultry supplier in the initial epidemic phase and accounted for 34.5% of human cases. Clade F emerged from a declining Clade E after the peak in human cases and was also associated with poultry. The emergence of Clade F was accompanied by the loss of integrated element CJIE5 and the acquisition of multiple blocks of recombination, likely from diverse ancestral C. jejuni lineages, and the loss of the methionine biosynthesis operon metAB. In contrast, Clades A-D were detected at low frequencies in human cases over the 14-year period of surveillance and were associated with multiple hosts. This longitudinal study sheds light on the evolutionary processes that result in strain emergence and differentiation, highlighting the role of horizontal gene transfer in the evolution and adaptation of this pathogen to new niches, and the subsequent impact on public health.

papers.title: EpiAlert: A Transparent CUSUM-EWMA Framework for Early Warning of Unusual Influenza-Like Illness Surveillance Activity
papers.abstract: Automated surveillance systems can prove to be extremely useful in detecting outbreaks of respiratory diseases that need further epidemiological investigation. In order for the system to be effective, careful attention has to be paid to the baseline used, absence of the observations, and the use of proper statistical methods. As a solution, the paper describes EpiAlert, a weekly surveillance system based on CDC FluView ILINet. The system is able to transform the number of ILI visits and the total number of visits into a ILI prevalence for the region, create the first reference from the three previous years using a +/- 2-week interval, transform the rate value, and apply two different detectors - CUSUM and EWMA. CUSUM is set at k=0.5 and h=5, whereas EWMA uses {lambda}=0.2 and H=2.7 values. Among the 55 districts, the system gives 45,138 pieces of information about the disease by transforming 44,297 pieces of data into alerts. It is found that there are 2,820 alerts in total (out of which 2,711 alerts used CUSUM, 402 used EWMA, and 293 used both detectors). Additionally, the experiments show that the sensitivity of the device depends greatly on the detector. The latest statistics can be tracked in the report for week 37 of 2026 that recently concluded in West.

papers.title: Does handgrip strength improve cardiometabolic risk stratification beyond detailed body composition? NHANES 2011-2014 with temporal validation
papers.abstract: Background: Handgrip strength is associated with cardiometabolic abnormalities, but whether it adds information once detailed adiposity and muscle mass are known is unclear. Methods: We studied adults aged 40-59 years from NHANES 2011-2012 (development, n=508) and 2013-2014 (temporal validation, n=616). The outcome was at least two of four non-adiposity abnormalities (elevated blood pressure, fasting glucose or triglycerides, or low HDL cholesterol); waist circumference was not part of the outcome. A prespecified feature ladder added DXA body fat percentage and visceral adipose tissue to age, sex, BMI and waist circumference (M1), then appendicular skeletal muscle index (M2), then absolute (M3A, primary) or weight-normalised (M3B) grip strength. Logistic regression was primary; elastic-net and XGBoost were supportive. Development performance used nested cross-validation; frozen models were scored once in the validation cohort. Paired increments used 2000 stratified bootstrap resamples. Results: The outcome occurred in 249 (49.0%) and 277 (45.0%) participants. Adding adiposity increased the logistic regression AUC by 0.0209 (95% CI 0.0024-0.0402) in development and 0.0209 (0.0032-0.0375) in temporal validation. Adding absolute grip strength to M2 changed the AUC by -0.0046 (-0.0107 to 0.0013) and 0.0045 (-0.0009 to 0.0098), respectively. All 12 grip-strength AUC increments across algorithms, definitions and cohorts had intervals that included zero. Calibration was unchanged and the incremental net benefit was not consistently positive. Model attributions to grip strength varied by algorithm. Conclusions: In middle-aged adults, detailed adiposity, but not grip strength, added reproducible information for concurrent cardiometabolic risk stratification beyond conventional anthropometry and muscle mass.

papers.title: A Novel Digital Phenotype of Physical Activity: Associations with Heart Rate Fragmentation
papers.abstract: BackgroundHeart rate fragmentation (HRF) has emerged as a novel marker of sinoatrial instability and neuroautonomic dysregulation and is a predictor of incident cardiovascular disease (CVD) events and cardiovascular mortality. Leveraging heart rate fragmentation as a novel measure may help us better understand the prognostic significance of physical activity. Physical activity (PA) patterns are multidimensional and difficult to study holistically, however. We sought to examine for novel PA clusters in a cohort of veteran men and evaluate their prognostic significance based on their associations with neuroautonomic dysregulation. MethodsIn this cross-sectional study, we examined 602 male veterans from the Vietnam Era Twins Study of Electrophysiology in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (VETS-EP) who were enrolled between 2022 and 2026. Accelerometry data were used to derive physical activity parameters across 6 domains: volume, sedentary behavior, intensity, diurnal pattern, fragmentation, and variability. Heart rate fragmentation was assessed using percentage of inflection points (PIP), inverse average length of segments (IALS), percentage of short segments (PSS), and percentage of alternating segments (PAS). Gaussian mixture models were used to derive digital phenotypes of physical activity, and associations with heart rate fragmentation were assessed using linear mixed models. ResultsParticipants had a mean age of 73.8 {+/-} 2.9 years and 93.2% reported White race. Two overlapping phenotypes of physical activity patterns were identified: a compact-early phenotype, characterized by earlier activity timing and slightly greater overall activity, and a diffuse-late phenotype, characterized by later activity timing and greater heterogeneity in activity volume. In fully adjusted models, the diffuse-late phenotype was associated with higher PIP, the primary outcome ({beta}: 1.199, 95% CI: 0.034 to 2.363, p-value: 0.044), and higher IALS ({beta}: 0.01210, 95% CI: 0.00048 to 0.02373, p-value: 0.041), but not PSS or PAS, compared with the compact-early phenotype. ConclusionsIn older male veterans, Gaussian mixture model phenotyping identified two overlapping physical activity phenotypes, differing mainly in diurnal timing and in the dispersion of overall activity, that were associated with modest differences in heart rate fragmentation. These phenotypes provide a framework for capturing complex physical activity patterns. Future prospective studies representing diverse populations are needed to validate such phenotypes.

papers.title: Mortality among Brazilian male police officers and firefighters over three decades
papers.abstract: BackgroundLong-term mortality data among Brazilian police officers and firefighters are scarce. This study investigated the leading causes of death in Brazilian male military police officers and firefighters over three decades, comparing their mortality and mean age at death with those of the male population. MethodsWe retrospectively analyzed death records of male military police officers and firefighters from Espirito Santo (ES), Brazil, from 1988 to 2019. Mortality was analyzed across three decades and the standardized mortality ratios (SMRs) for the three leading causes were calculated using the male populations of ES and Brazil as references. ResultsOverall, 2,198 deaths were identified, with a mean age at death of 59 {+/-} 18.5 years, compared with 60.5 {+/-} 23.9 years among men in ES and 63.4 {+/-} 23.7 years among Brazilian men. Mean age at death was 36 {+/-} 9 years among active-duty and 68 {+/-} 13 years among inactive personnel. Across the study population, the leading causes of death were circulatory system diseases (32%), external causes (26%) and neoplasms (15%). Circulatory disease mortality was higher in the second and third decades compared with both reference populations, whereas external-cause mortality shifted from higher, in the first two decades, to lower than expected in the last decade. Neoplasm mortality was higher relative to Brazil only in the last decade. ConclusionMortality patterns differed by cause and over time. The younger mean age at death among active-duty personnel, together with cause-specific excess mortality, highlights the importance of long-term occupational health surveillance and preventive strategies.

papers.title: Integrating Longitudinal Cohorts for Population Health Research: Mainland and Island-based Puerto Rican Diabetes Study
papers.abstract: Background Population research increasingly relies on integrating data across studies to understand patterns of health and disease at broader scales. Such integration expands sample size and supports multimodal analyses, but independent cohort studies are often not directly comparable due to differences in instruments, timing, and measurement structure. Data harmonization addresses this challenge by transforming heterogeneous variables into comparable measures, allowing datasets collected under different protocols to be analyzed jointly, but published harmonization efforts seldom include an analysis conducted on the integrated dataset itself. Methods We developed an integrated dataset, combining two longitudinal cohorts, the Boston Puerto Rican Health Study (BPRHS) and the Puerto Rico Observational Study of Psychosocial, Environmental, and Chronic Disease Trends (PROSPECT). Comparability between variables was established through an explicit framework distinguishing availability from construct comparability, and the evidence supporting comparability is reported by class of feature, including tests of measurement invariance and differential test functioning for the multi-item psychosocial scales. To support transparency and reuse, we provide an open-source Python pipeline and structured metadata describing variable alignment and transformations. As a worked example of downstream use, we conducted a Random Forest analysis predicting diabetes status. Results The integrated dataset comprises 539 harmonized variables across four BPRHS visits and two PROSPECT visits, each documented with its source variable, question wording, and transformation. In the worked example, the integrated dataset retained predictive signal relative to cohort-specific models and improved performance for the smaller cohort. Conclusions These findings illustrate how transparent, documented cross-cohort integration can support predictive population health research while making the basis for comparability explicit.

papers.title: Longitudinal personal environmental exposure and Streptococcus pneumoniae colonisation in a cohort of children 5-14 years old in rural Gambia.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Air pollution contributes substantially to morbidity and mortality in low-income countries, where reliance on solid fuels leads to high levels of household exposure. Colonisation of the upper respiratory tract by Streptococcus pneumoniae is a prerequisite for pneumococcal disease, and inhaled air pollutants may influence colonisation through impaired mucociliary clearance. Therefore, we investigated the association between S. pneumoniae colonisation and personal exposure to particulate matter (PM2.5) and carbon monoxide (CO) as well as temperature and relative humidity in older children in The Gambia. Methods We conducted a prospective study of 134 children aged 5-14 years across eight visits in rural Gambia. Personal 24-hour PM2.5, CO, temperature and relative humidity exposures were measured using personal monitors. Concurrently, combined nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal swabs were collected at each visit, and S. pneumoniae colonisation was determined by microbiological culture. Mixed-effects logistic regression models were used to examine associations between environmental exposures and colonisation. Exposures were additionally decomposed into between-child and within-child components. Models were adjusted for age, season, and household income tertile. Results A total of 554 child visits with paired exposure and microbiological data were analysed. Overall, 24-hour geometric mean PM2.5 and CO were 12.6 {micro}g/m3 (95% CI 12.2-13.1) and 0.16 ppm (95% CI 0.14-0.19) respectively and overall S. pneumoniae colonisation prevalence was 39.7%. In conventional models, PM2.5, CO, temperature, and relative humidity were not significantly associated with S. pneumoniae colonisation after adjustment for confounders. In the within-between decomposition analysis, higher between-child temperature exposure was consistently associated with lower odds of colonisation (mutually adjusted model: OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.56-0.98; p = 0.034). Relative humidity showed an inverse within-child association in crude analysis (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.52-0.93; p = 0.013), which attenuated after adjustment for season and other confounders. No associations were observed for PM2.5 or CO exposures. Conclusion At the exposure levels observed in this cohort of older children, PM2.5 and CO exposures were not independently associated with S. pneumoniae colonisation. The pattern observed for temperature suggests that longer-term temperature conditions may be more relevant to pneumococcal colonisation than short-term exposure variation in this setting.

papers.title: Impact of Prolonged Obesity Across the Lifecourse on Myocardial Stress and Injury in Older Age: Birth Cohort Study
papers.abstract: Background The consequences of prolonged exposure to obesity on biomarkers of myocardial stress and injury remain unclear. We examined associations of duration and cumulative severity of obesity from childhood to later adulthood with concentrations of N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI), and growth differentiation factor-15 (GDF-15) at age 62 years. Methods The sample comprised 4,901 participants in the 1958 National Child Development Study who had measurements of NT-proBNP, hs-cTnI, or GDF-15 at age 62 years and at least four BMI assessments between 7 and 62 years of age. Individual BMI trajectories were modelled, from which total duration of obesity and mean excess BMI (area between the trajectory and the age-specific obesity threshold divided by duration) were derived. Associations of ever versus never having been obese, obesity duration, and mean excess BMI with biomarker concentrations were examined using general linear regression models with progressive adjustment for early-life characteristics; contemporaneous cardiometabolic factors; and health behaviours, socioeconomic position, and psychosocial factors. Nonlinear associations of obesity duration were estimated using restricted cubic splines and subsequently approximated using linear splines. Results Overall, 26.3% of participants had ever experienced obesity. There was no evidence of an association between ever versus never having been obese and NT-proBNP. Among men, ever having been obese was associated with 11.00% (95% CI, 4.62-17.37) higher hs-cTnI in the fully adjusted model, whereas there was no evidence of an association among women. Ever having been obese was associated with higher GDF-15, although the association attenuated substantially after adjustment for contemporaneous cardiometabolic factors. Longer obesity duration was associated with higher concentrations of all three biomarkers in fully adjusted models, but the pattern differed by biomarker: hs-cTnI increased approximately linearly with duration, whereas NT-proBNP and GDF-15 remained relatively stable up to approximately 25 years of obesity before increasing with longer duration. In fully adjusted models, each additional year of obesity beyond 25 years was associated with 1.80% (95% CI, 0.54-3.06) higher NT-proBNP and 0.81% (95% CI, 0.25-1.36) higher GDF-15, while each additional year across the full range of obesity duration was associated with 0.41% (95% CI, 0.07-0.76) higher hs-cTnI. Among participants who had ever experienced obesity, each 1 kg/m2 higher mean excess BMI was associated with 4.02% (95% CI, 1.79-6.24) higher NT-proBNP and 2.00% (95% CI, 0.49-3.51) higher hs-cTnI in fully adjusted models; there was no evidence of an association with GDF-15. Conclusions Longer duration of obesity was associated with higher concentrations of biomarkers reflecting myocardial stress, injury, and cellular stress at age 62 years, with associations particularly evident after approximately 25 years of obesity for NT-proBNP and GDF-15. These findings suggest that duration of obesity may provide clinically relevant information beyond current obesity status, supporting its consideration as an additional dimension of cumulative obesity burden in cardiovascular risk assessment.

papers.title: Quantifying Systematic Bias in Observational Causal Estimates Using Negative Controls: The Bias Attribution Fraction
papers.abstract: Importance. Observational studies dominate evidence in cardiovascular outcomes research, yet no widely adopted reporting standard requires authors to disclose how much of an observed association is attributable to systematic error. The negative-control calibration framework of the Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics consortium returns a binary answer: a calibrated P-value either crosses 0.05 or it does not. That answer conflates "is there a signal" with "is the signal credible." Objective. To define the Bias Attribution Fraction (BAF), a continuous estimator in [0, 1] that quantifies the fraction of an observed log relative risk that is attributable to systematic bias, together with its 95% credible interval, and to evaluate whether reporting calibrated P-value plus BAF plus interval width produces more defensible decisions than reporting the calibrated P-value alone. Design. Three-part study: (i) metric definition and interval construction; (ii) Monte Carlo simulation across 1920 conditions by 1000 repetitions = 1,920,000 simulated target estimates (a primary grid plus a sign-flipped companion grid of identical size, pooled for all analyses), with truth known by construction; (iii) two-arm beta-blocker target trial emulation in MIMIC IV, adhering to the TARGET guideline, with targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) and 12 negative-control outcomes. Setting. MIMIC IV (critical care) and MIMIC IV ECG, 2008 to 2019. Participants. Adults with a first intensive care unit stay and a recorded 12-lead ECG. Exposures. Two clinical questions are evaluated: (1) reaching at least 50% of guideline-recommended target dose of an index beta-blocker within 7 days of admission, sustained to 12 months, versus lower or no exposure; (2) receiving guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) with at least two of three foundational drug classes at adequate dose for 12 months versus fewer. Main Outcomes and Measures. One-year all-cause mortality. Primary analytic outputs: (i) the calibrated P-value from a negative-control empirical null distribution with 12 outcomes; (ii) BAF-hat with a Markov chain Monte Carlo 95% credible interval; (iii) a verdict drawn from a truth-calibrated lookup table mapping the BAF-hat by interval-width cell to a probability of being bias-dominated. Results. Across 1,920,000 simulated repetitions, the calibrated P-value alone yielded a misuse rate (declared usable while truth was bias-dominated) of 36.02%. Adding the BAF point estimate reduced misuse to 16.48%, and requiring the whole credible interval of BAF to lie below 0.5, clear of the bias-dominated zone, reduced misuse to 10.16%. Requiring in addition a calibrated probability of bias dominance below 15% reduced misuse to 3.02% at the cost of declaring 22.1% of estimates usable (versus 61.8% for the calibrated P-value alone). Read from the bias-dominated view, meaning that withholding a repetition is a positive call and being truly bias-dominated is a positive truth, the BAF estimator achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.922, compared with 0.787 for the calibrated P-value. In MIMIC IV, question 1 produced a calibrated P-value of 0.894 and BAF-hat = 0.875 (95% credible interval 0.385 to 0.992); the apparent one-year mortality reduction of 16.9% was entirely attributable to systematic bias and the association was not usable as effect evidence. Question 2 also failed layer 1, with a calibrated P-value of 0.1026, and BAF-hat = 0.460 placed it in the "competitive, no verdict" zone. Conclusions and Relevance. Pairing the calibrated P-value with BAF and its 95% credible interval turns a binary credibility judgement into a three-channel report (signal existence, effect size, and bias fraction). Despite TARGET-adherent design, doubly robust TMLE, and 12 negative controls, both clinical questions in this study still failed to qualify as effect evidence, with question 1 demonstrating complete bias domination and BAF quantifying the systematic error that remained. The reporting standard proposed here can be applied to any observational study that includes negative controls, without requiring additional data.

papers.title: MID-LIFE LEISURE-TIME PHYSICAL ACTIVITY IS ASSOCIATED WITH LOWER HIP FRACTURE RISK IN UK BIOBANK
papers.abstract: Leisure time physical activity (LTPA) in mid-life may have beneficial effects on risk factors for hip fracture in later life. Conversely, physical activity may increase fracture risk through risk of injury, and the optimal amount of physical activity for reducing hip fracture risk remains unclear. We explored the associations between volume and intensity of LTPA in mid-life, and subsequent risk of hip fracture ascertained from linked health data. This prospective observational study used middle aged adults aged 40- 65 years from UK Biobank. LTPA volume (LTPAv) was derived from self-reported walking, moderate and vigorous activity at baseline (2006- 2010). Cox proportional hazard and Fine-Gray sub-distribution models were used to estimate the association between activity and hip fracture, which was sex-stratified. From 324,284 participants with complete data 53% were female and mean age at baseline was 54.5 (SD 7.3). Across 16 years of follow-up there were 2,674 hip fractures. In terms of LTPA volume, the lowest risk of hip fracture occurred in quintile 3 for women (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.67-0.91), and men (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.60- 0.90), relating to approximately one hour/day of leisure time physical activity. When activity intensities were examined separately, the lowest estimated hazards were observed for vigorous activity, at quintile 4 in women (HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.55 - 0.76) and quintile 3 in men (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.52- 0.79), corresponding to approximately 60- 90 minutes of vigorous activity per week. In conclusion, moderately high volumes of mid-life physical activity, particularly vigorous activity, were related to lower risk of subsequent hip fracture, but these relationships appear to attenuate at higher volumes.

papers.title: Carbonaceous Components Underlying Wildfire Smoke PM2.5-Associated Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias in Older US Adults
papers.abstract: Wildfire smoke exposure is increasing across the U.S., but the long-term neurological effects of smoke-specific fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and its carbonaceous components remain uncertain. Using Medicare data from 2002 through 2019, we examined incident Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) among 39,678,630 fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries followed from 2005 through 2019. We identified 3,501,414 incident AD cases over 258.5 million person-years and 8,377,416 incident ADRD cases over 248.6 million person-years. We linked the cohort with annual, high-resolution estimates of smoke and non-smoke PM2.5 mass and carbonaceous components (elemental and organic carbon) and fitted stratified Cox proportional hazards models. Per 1 g/m3 increase, smoke PM2.5 was associated with incident AD (hazard ratio [HR], 1.015, 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.005-1.026) and ADRD (1.029 [1.024-1.035]). Smoke carbonaceous fraction was also associated with AD (1.063 [1.042-1.085]) and ADRD (1.090 [1.077-1.103]). Within the ADRD endpoint, smoke-related associations exceeded their corresponding non-smoke associations on a per-unit-mass basis. Per interquartile range, associations were smaller for smoke PM2.5 (AD, 1.005 [1.002-1.008]; ADRD, 1.009 [1.008-1.011]) than for non-smoke PM2.5 (AD, 1.086 [1.079-1.094]; ADRD, 1.048 [1.043-1.053]). Associations varied across geographic, racial, socioeconomic, and clinical subgroups. Long-term wildfire smoke exposure, particularly its carbonaceous fraction, was associated with higher incidence of AD and ADRD among older U.S. adults. The associations correspond to 2,284 and 11,142 incident cases per year of AD and ADRD attributable to smoke PM2.5 among older Medicare beneficiaries, with the carbonaceous fraction accounting for most of this burden. These findings support the use of source-resolved and composition-specific smoke metrics in dementia research and wildfire-smoke health-impact assessments.

papers.title: The transition to retirement and dementia risk: An application of sequence analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundRetirement is a major life transition that may influence cognitive aging. Retirement pathways are becoming increasingly diversified, yet evidence on how heterogeneous retirement trajectories relate to dementia risk remains limited. This study used sequence and cluster analysis to characterize thousands of transition-to-retirement trajectories, including retirement timing and work intensity, to estimate associations with dementia risk. MethodsWe used data from 13,879 participants in the U.S. Health and Retirement Study. Our exposure was transition-to-retirement trajectories between ages 51 and 75 identified using sequence and cluster analysis. Our outcome was a validated algorithmically derived dementia probability measure. We estimated associations between trajectory clusters and dementia risk beginning at age 76 using generalized estimating equations, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. Inverse probability weights were used to account for attrition. ResultsWe identified ten distinct transition-to-retirement trajectories characterized by differences in timing of retirement, part-time work, disability, and labor force attachment. Compared with individuals retiring after full-time work in their early-to-mid 60s, dementia risk was similar among those retiring earlier or later from full-time work. In contrast, individuals with sustained part-time employment between ages 51 and 75 had lower odds of dementia (OR: 0.62, 95% CI: 0.48, 0.80), while trajectories characterized by prolonged disability were associated with higher odds of dementia (OR: 1.53, 95% CI: 1.22, 1.91). ConclusionsRetirement timing alone showed limited association with later-life dementia risk, whereas sustained part-time employment and disability-related trajectories were more strongly associated with dementia risk. These findings suggest that employment intensity and health-related exit from the labor force may be more relevant for dementia risk than retirement timing, and that gradual and flexible work-to-retirement transitions may benefit brain health.

papers.title: Associations between commonly consumed beverages and the oral microbiome in three US cohort studies
papers.abstract: Multiple external factors shape human microbial communities. Beverages represent particularly frequent dietary exposures that may impact oral microbiome composition. We examined associations of coffee, tea, alcohol, sugar-sweetened beverages, artificially-sweetened beverages, and fruit juice consumption with the oral microbiome in three large cohort studies (n=5,598). Beverage consumption was assessed by food frequency questionnaire and categorized as non-consumers and tertiles of intake among consumers, except fruit juice, which was categorized into quartiles. DNA from oral wash specimens was sequenced (16S rRNA, V4 region). Associations with alpha and beta diversity and individual genera were assessed using multivariable linear, logistic, count-based regression models and weighted permutation-based models accounting for multiple comparisons in genus-level analyses. Only alcoholic beverage consumption was associated with all alpha diversity metrics; the highest tertile of alcohol drinking was associated with 10.18 (95% CI: 5.56, 14.80) greater observed amplicon sequence variants vs. non-consumers. All beverages accounted for 4.06% of variability in beta diversity (unweighted UniFrac); in univariable models, alcoholic beverages had the largest R{superscript 2} among individual beverages (0.86%) and accounted for the majority (25/28, 89.3%) of genus-level associations, mostly with beer and liquor. For example, high alcoholic beverage intake (T3 vs. non-consumers) was associated with 2.25 and 2.17 times the odds of having Megasphaera and Peptostreptococcus, respectively, and 23% lower abundance of Lautropia. Alcoholic beverage consumption was strongly associated with oral microbes, including taxa linked to poor oral health; these findings suggest that alcohol-associated differences in the oral microbiome may have implications for oral and systemic health.

papers.title: Burden of Non-Communicable Diseases Attributable to Polygenic Risk and Its Association with Healthcare Utilization in Taiwan
papers.abstract: BackgroundNon-communicable diseases (NCDs) impose substantial population burden. Their polygenic architecture informs early risk stratification through polygenic risk scores (PRS). Previous studies reported elevated-PRS burden comparable to some modifiable risk factors (MRFs), yet evidence remains confined to European populations. We quantified the PRS-attributable NCD burden in Taiwan. MethodsLinking Taiwan Biobank and National Health Insurance Research Database (N {approx} 140K), we analyzed 42 high-burden NCDs. Elevated genetic risk (PRSe; top 10%) was assessed using Cox models. We estimated population attributable fractions (PAFs) and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) using Taiwan-specific estimates from Global Burden of Disease 2023, and examined associations between an integrated PRS (iPRS) and healthcare utilization. FindingsStrongest PRSe associations occurred for atrial fibrillation (AFib; HR = 3.56 [95% CI: 3.23-3.92]) and gout (2.41 [2.33-2.49]), yielding PAFs of 20% and 12%, respectively, while population-level attributable DALYs were largest for type 2 diabetes (T2D), intracranial hemorrhage (ICH), and lung cancer. At the individual level, PRSe corresponded to 1.50 [1.42-1.57] healthy life-years lost for T2D and 0.57 [0.40-0.76] for ICH, approaching 2.4 years for the top 1% PRS. Polygenic attributable burden was overall greater in men. For several diseases, PRSe-associated PAF and DALYs exceeded those of individual MRFs (e.g., smoking, alcohol use). Top-decile iPRS was linked to 23.9% (15.0-33.6%) more hospital days, 19.1% (13.2-25.3%) more inpatient visits, and 9.6% (6.9-12.4%) more outpatient visits. InterpretationPolygenic risk accounts for a measurable--and for several diseases, MRF-comparable--share of NCD burden in Taiwan, providing a quantitative foundation for integrating genetic liability into preventive care and health planning. FundingNational Taiwan University Academic Research-Career Development Project, Yushan Young Fellow Program from the Ministry of Education (MoE), and the Population Health Research Center from Featured Areas Research Center Program within the framework of the Higher Education Sprout Project by the MoE in Taiwan.

papers.title: Seasonally Normalized Vitamin D Status and Long-Term Mortality and Multisystem Disease Risk in the UK Biobank
papers.abstract: BackgroundVitamin D deficiency has been associated with mortality and chronic disease. In a recent study of Israeli Leumit Health Services (LHS) and US TriNetX populations, severe deficiency was reproducibly associated with mortality and multisystem morbidity, while longitudinal supplementation reconstructed from pharmacy dispensing was associated with lower risk. MethodsWe sought to reproduce these associations and address a wide range of potential confounders in the deeply phenotyped UK Biobank. Baseline circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] was standardized to a common late-winter nadir using an eight-harmonic model, and participants were categorized according to nadir-equivalent 25(OH)D as <5, 5-10, 10-15, 15-20, or [≥]20 ng/mL. Primary survival analyses used one-year delayed entry and complete-case multivariable adjustment. ResultsAnalyses included 412,020 participants and 31,197 deaths. Mortality hazard ratios were 2.03 (95% CI 1.90-2.18), 1.34 (1.29-1.39), 1.08 (1.04-1.11), respectively, for <5, 5-10 and 10-15, versus [≥]20 ng/mL. Associations previously observed in LHS and TriNetX were reproduced, notably for diabetes, myocardial infarction, cerebrovascular disease, dementia, diabetic retinopathy, and end-stage renal disease, whereas skin malignancies showed the opposite gradient, consistent with greater ultraviolet exposure. DAG-informed causal analyses using generalized overlap weighting achieved acceptable balance across measured covariates; weighted 10-year mortality was 9.7% with very severe deficiency versus 4.8% with [≥]20 ng/mL, supporting a causal interpretation. Estimates remained stable with landmark lags extending to 5 years after measurement. ConclusionsSeasonally normalized 25(OH)D identifies a reproducible state of systemic vulnerability while reducing exposure misclassification caused by calendar timing of measurement. An interactive implementation of the normalization model is available: https://vitamind.medil.ai.

papers.title: Life-course patterns of heavy menstrual bleeding and menstrual pain across multiple population-based cohorts
papers.abstract: BackgroundHeavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) and menstrual pain (MP) are among the most common menstrual cycle related symptoms with substantial impacts on quality of life. Despite this, population-level evidence on their prevalence across the life course is scarce. MethodsWe conducted descriptive analyses of six longitudinal population-based cohorts from the United Kingdom, United States, Norway, and Australia. We estimated cumulative prevalence (across all available timepoints) and age-specific point prevalence of HMB and MP. Cumulative prevalence estimates were stratified by sociodemographic factors, where data permitted. We also examined HMB and MP incidence in adolescent cohorts with repeated measurements. FindingsHMB and MP are commonly reported, with cumulative prevalence across all the cohorts and timepoints (i.e., ever reported) ranging from 36% to 89% for HMB and 46% to 72% for MP. In adolescence, MP (point-prevalence: 33% to 47%) is more commonly reported than HMB (16% to 24%), whereas in later ages (45 years and above), HMB (47% to 70%) is more prevalent than MP (24% to 40%). We found no consistent evidence that symptoms were more likely to co-occur than occur independently; patterns varied across life stages and cohorts. Symptoms were more common in those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds and minoritised ethnic groups. Incidence of both HMP and MP peaked in the years immediately following menarche. InterpretationMost women experience heavy and/or painful periods at some point. MP is more common in adolescence and HMB in later reproductive life. Generating robust life-course evidence on menstrual symptom patterns is essential to inform clinical guidelines, reduce diagnostic delays, and address inequalities in menstrual health.

papers.title: Inflammation-Related Biomarkers Linking Environmental Chemical Mixtures and Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease: A Population-Based Study from NHANES 1999-2020
papers.abstract: ObjectiveEnvironmental pollutants are increasingly recognized as potential risk factors for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), yet the effects of mixed exposures and underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We evaluated associations between environmental chemical mixtures and MASLD and the mediating role of inflammation-related biomarkers. MethodsWe analyzed 60 environmental chemicals across six categories among 39,061 U.S. adults from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 1999-2020. Principal Component Pursuit with Principal Component Analysis (PCP-PCA) identified latent exposure patterns. MASLD was identified using multisociety Delphi consensus criteria and the Hepatic Steatosis Index (HSI [≥] 36). Logistic regression, restricted cubic spline models, and mediation analysis were applied. ResultsPCP-PCA generated 5-17 dimensions per chemical category, with first-dimension variance contributions ranging from 30.70% to 98.88%. Six dimensions from four categories were retained, with phthalate esters (PAEs) and organophosphate flame retardants (OPFRs) showing the most consistent associations with MASLD. PAEs Dim.1, explaining 90.71% of variance, showed a significant non-linear dose-response association (P-nonlinear = 0.0001). Significant associations were identified for mono-isobutyl phthalate (MiBP; OR 1.12, 95% CI 1.07-1.19), mono(carboxyoctyl) phthalate (MCOP; OR 1.08, 95% CI 1.02-1.14), mono(carboxynonyl) phthalate (MCNP; OR 1.12, 95% CI 1.03-1.21), and bis(1,3-dichloro-2-propyl) phosphate (BDCP; OR 1.15, 95% CI 1.08-1.23). C-reactive protein (CRP) and red cell distribution width (RDW) were the primary mediators, accounting for 32.42% and 19.62% of the MiBP-MASLD association, respectively (both p < 0.0001). ConclusionEnvironmental co-exposure, particularly to PAEs and OPFRs, was associated with higher MASLD risk, with systemic inflammation potentially contributing to these associations.

papers.title: The Gut Microbiome-Amino Acid Pathway to Emotional Lability: A Multi-Step Mendelian Randomization Study
papers.abstract: Emotional lability (EL) is a prevalent cross-diagnostic symptom with unclear etiology. Given the potential role of the gut-brain axis in linking gut microbiota to EL, we adopted a multi-step Mendelian randomization (MR) framework to investigate the causal effects of gut microbiota on EL and the mediating role of blood metabolites. Bidirectional two-sample MR was first implemented to determine the causal relationship and direction between gut microbiota and EL, followed by multivariable MR (MVMR) to assess the direct contributions of individual microbial taxa. We then applied a multistep MR approach to identify gut microbiota specifically associated with EL-related psychopathology. Finally, the mediation effects of blood metabolites were quantified via the coefficient of variation method, and pathway analysis was conducted to verify the biological plausibility of the enriched metabolic pathways. Bidirectional MR detected 16 gut microbiota species associated with EL risk. MVMR identified three causally associated bacteria: RUG013 sp001486445 exerted the strongest positive effect (odds ratio [OR] = 1.570, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.090-2.261, P = 0.015), followed by CAG-485 sp002362485 (OR = 1.323, 95% CI: 1.080-1.619, P = 0.006). Each standard deviation (SD) increment in CAG-485 sp002362485 was linked to a 32.3% higher risk of EL. This bacterium was specific to EL and correlated with glycine/serine/threonine metabolites. Reverse MR analyses ruled out reverse causality. Author summaryEmotional lability--defined as frequent, rapid shifts in mood and emotional state--is a pervasive symptom across many psychiatric disorders, and it is associated with poorer treatment outcomes and higher risks of self-harm. Despite its clinical significance, the biological causes of emotional lability remain largely unknown. Accumulating evidence points to a link between the gut microbiota (the community of microbes living in the human digestive tract) and brain function via the gut-brain axis, but it has remained unclear whether gut microbes directly cause changes in emotional stability, and what biological pathways might mediate such effects. To answer these questions, we employed a multi-step Mendelian randomization approach. This method uses natural genetic variation as a tool to help distinguish causal relationships from simple correlations, reducing bias from confounding factors. We first tested the causal link between gut microbiota and emotional lability, then identified microbial markers specific to emotional lability by comparing them with other common psychiatric disorders. Finally, we investigated whether blood metabolites act as intermediate messengers that connect gut microbial activity to emotional regulation. We identified 16 gut bacterial species that causally influence susceptibility to emotional lability, with three showing independent effects: two bacteria increase risk, while one is protective. The strongest risk-associated bacterium, CAG-485 sp002362485, was found to act in part by disrupting amino acid metabolism, particularly pathways involving glycine, serine, and threonine. We also confirmed that the effect flows from gut microbiota to emotional state, rather than emotional changes altering the gut microbiome. These findings clarify the causal role of gut microbiota in emotional dysregulation and reveal key metabolic pathways that underpin the gut-brain connection. They not only improve our understanding of why emotional lability occurs, but also suggest new potential strategies for intervention, such as targeting gut microbes or related metabolic processes.

papers.title: Surveillance of bacterial and fungal infections in hospitalised COVID-19 patients: an ISARIC/WHO CCP-UK and UKHSA linkage study
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo characterise COVID-19 inpatients with and without bacterial/fungal preceding, co- and secondary infections, and describe the distribution of organisms associated with COVID-19 and antibiotic use. MethodsWe linked ISARIC/WHO CCP-UK data from hospitals in England (admissions 01/01/2020-18/10/2021) with UK Health Security Agency infections datasets of COVID-19, and bacterial- and fungal-positive specimens using a multi-step hierarchical algorithm. We retained those aged >18 years and categorised COVID-19-associated infection as preceding (2-28 days prior to SARS-CoV-2 PCR positive date), co-infection ({+/-}1 day) or secondary (2-28 days after). ResultsDuring the study period, there were 173,947 hospitalised episodes of COVID-19; 5.8% (n=10,017) with a bacterial or fungal preceding, co- or secondary infection. Preceding and co-infections were rare (preceding: 0.7%; co-infection: 1.5%) while secondary infections were more common (3.5%). Escherichia coli (29.6%) and Staphylococcus aureus (15.2%) were the most identified organisms in blood specimens, while S. aureus (22.9%) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (20.4%) were most common in lower respiratory tract specimens. The 28-day case fatality rate (CFR) remained static (36%) in those with secondary infection, whereas it decreased between early 2020 and mid-2021 in the other infection groups (37% to 27%). Of those with no positive microbiology, 72.8% received antibiotics, though this decreased between January-June 2020 (77.6%) and April-October 2021 (62.6%). ConclusionBacterial and fungal infections complicated approximately 1-in-17 hospitalised episodes of COVID-19, with CFR of >25%. Antibiotic prescribing was common in those without firm evidence of bacterial infection. We recommend adhering to NICE guidance which discourages empirical antibiotic use for hospitalised COVID-19 patients.

papers.title: Cardiovascular and cancer mortality inversely associated with long-term ambient ultraviolet exposure across US Health Service Areas with UK Biobank corroboration
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVETo assess associations of ambient UV with cardiovascular and cancer mortality across US Health Service Areas (HSAs), prioritise outcomes by signal and attributable burden, assess racial and ethnic variation, with UK Biobank corroboration. DESIGNEcological analysis of HSAs using linear regression of crude mortality on ambient UV and social vulnerability, with correction for multiple comparisons. SETTINGUS HSAs and UK Biobank. DATA SOURCESPublicly available US data and UK Biobank data accessed under Application 82526. PARTICIPANTS704 808 annual cardiovascular deaths (aged [≥]65) and 565 287 annual cancer deaths (aged [≥]50) from populations of 52.8 and 115.2 million; UK Biobank analyses included 412 665 individuals. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURESCardiovascular, all-cancer, and body-site-specific cancer mortality; regression slope per interquartile-range increase in UV ({beta} UV/IQR), modelled attributable burden for US data, and hazard ratios for the UK Biobank data. RESULTSHigher UV was associated with lower cardiovascular ({beta}UV/IQR -68.3 deaths/100 000; P<0.001) and all-cancer mortality (-43.2; P<0.001), corresponding to 36 043 (5.1%) and 49 789 (8.8%) fewer US deaths annually, respectively. Associations varied by race and ethnicity. Cardiovascular findings were directionally consistent between US and UK datasets. All-cancer mortality and 10 of 18 cancers were inversely associated with UV in the US; UK analyses found inverse associations for all-cancer and two individual body-site-specific cancers. Twelve cancers showed directionally concordant associations across the datasets, of which ten were inverse. Lung cancer showed the strongest inverse association in each dataset. CONCLUSIONSHigher UV was associated with lower cardiovascular and cancer mortality across US HSAs, with modelled attributable burdens exceeding 5%; UK Biobank findings provided partial corroboration. Twelve of 18 site-specific cancers were directionally concordant between datasets. US race-stratified heterogeneity did not follow a skin-colour gradient, suggesting residual confounding. WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPICAlthough intermittent ultraviolet (UV) exposure is associated with risk of increased skin-cancer incidence including keratinocyte cancers and melanoma, there is no parallel increase in mortality. In contrast, long-term ecological and cohort studies have consistently associated higher UV exposure and sun-seeking behaviour with lower all-cause, cardiovascular, and internal cancer mortality. While large-scale randomised placebo-controlled trials of vitamin D supplements have all failed their primary endpoints to reduce incidence or mortality, shifting attention toward other UV-induced pathways that may better explain the observed net benefits. Complementary clinical evidence comes from NB-UVB phototherapy, a controlled surrogate of solar UV, which provides mechanistic insight through its association with reduced cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events and its guideline-directed role in dermatological conditions and early-stage cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. What this study addsThis study provides updated nationwide estimates of the association between long-term ambient ultraviolet radiation and mortality across US Health Service Area and UK Biobank datasets, showing inverse associations with two of the leading causes of death: cardiovascular disease and cancer. Across the observed US interquartile range of ambient UV, higher UV was associated with 36,043 fewer cardiovascular deaths and 49,789 fewer cancer deaths per year, with inverse cancer associations observed across multiple internal cancers and directionally corroborated in an independent UK Biobank dataset across all-cancer and 12 of 18 individual site-cancers. Prespecified racial subgroup analyses showed that UV-mortality relationships were heterogeneous and non-monotonic across racial groups, rather than following the expected gradient by skin colour seen in clinical phototherapy. This suggests that UV-mortality associations may be shaped by additional biological, behavioural, environmental, or social determinants not fully captured by the Social Vulnerability Index.

papers.title: Cell-Cell Communication Patterns in Alzheimer's Disease Differ by Cortical Layer
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTIONExisting cell-cell communication (CCC) studies of Alzheimers disease dementia (ADD) using cortical snRNAseq data do not account for the distinct cell-type and gene-expression profiles within cortical layers. Cortical-layer-aware CCC analysis may clarify biological mechanisms associated with ADD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI). METHODSWe applied our recent analytical tool STACCato to identify CCC events associated with ADD and MCI within cortical layers, using a large-scale prefrontal cortex snRNAseq dataset ([~]1.4M nuclei, n=395) with cortical layers annotated from reference spatial transcriptomics data. RESULTSWe identified ADD/MCI-related CCC events with distinct patterns within cortical layers, including ADD-related interactions involving the known AD risk genes APOE and APP that were detected only in microglia in layer 5, and those with opposite effects of ADD and MCI in layers 5 and 6. DISCUSSIONOur findings on cortical-layer-aware ADD/MCI-related CCC events underscore the importance of spatially-aware genomics studies of AD.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving, Decentralised Inference of Epidemic Transmission Dynamics from Digital Exposure Histories
papers.abstract: BackgroundExposure-history data collected during epidemics or pandemics within digital contact-tracing applications hold immense potential for rapid, scalable epidemiological inference. The sensitivity of these data makes privacy-preserving designs essential to secure public trust and app uptake. However, during the COVID-19 pandemic, such approaches were not yet available at the scale or maturity required for deployment. We present a Bayesian decentralised framework to infer transmission dynamics from exposure-history data while protecting user privacy. MethodsOur approach is based on iterative communication between user devices and a central server, computing log-likelihood gradients on device from exposure-history data and centrally updating parameter values using only aggregated gradients. Applying this framework to synthetic exposure-history data from a hypothetical respiratory pathogen epidemic simulated on dynamic contact networks, we assessed its ability to estimate the underlying transmission parameters, perform infector attribution, and reconstruct serial-interval (SI) distributions. We systematically explored how inference was affected by incomplete exposure-history data arising from partial app adoption, case under-ascertainment, and incomplete exposure logging, and by transmission scenarios. FindingsOur decentralised framework accurately recovered transmission parameters, closely matching estimates derived from centralised data with no systematic bias in posterior means. Parameter recovery remained robust when hazards from unobserved exposures were known as a daily average across the population. Although incomplete exposure-history data and specific transmission scenarios introduced compensatory parameter biases, the inferred host infectiousness profile retained sufficient accuracy, and the weekly SI distributions reconstructed from infector attributions closely resembled the ground-truth distributions. InterpretationOur findings highlight that, beyond its primary role as a control measure, digital contact tracing could help characterise transmission dynamics almost in real time and inform public health interventions while preserving user privacy. FundingOxford Martin School Programme on Digital Pandemic Preparedness; National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Health Protection Research Unit in Emerging and Zoonotic Infections. Evidence before this studyWe searched PubMed for studies published from database inception to Sept 30, 2026, using the keywords ("digital contact tracing" OR "exposure notification" OR "contact tracing app") AND ("federated learning" OR "decentralised" OR "privacy-preserving" OR "statistical inference" OR "Bayesian inference") AND ("transmission" OR "serial interval" OR "infectiousness"). During the COVID-19 pandemic, digital contact-tracing (DCT) apps were deployed at an unprecedented scale: 224 COVID-19 apps were launched across 127 countries, 128 of which supported exposure notification. In England and Wales, the NHS COVID-19 app had 16.5 million regular users (28% of the total population) and averted an estimated 1 million cases and 9,600 deaths in its first year. To protect privacy, however, most apps used decentralised architectures that kept exposure-history data on users devices. This privacy-preserving principle has largely prevented these data from being used for epidemiological inference to understand transmission dynamics, such as estimating the serial-interval (SI) distribution and host infectiousness profile over time. While existing decentralised algorithms estimate each users infection risk, we found no study that developed and evaluated a framework for estimating population-level epidemiological parameters from exposure-history data that remain on users devices. Added value of this studyTo our knowledge, this is the first such framework. It estimates key quantities required for understanding transmission dynamics, including how an infected individuals infectiousness changes over time relative to their symptom onset date, how much close contacts increase the risk of transmission, and the SI distribution. The framework learns an exposure hazard function from data that never leave users devices, then attributes infections to likely infectors, and reconstructs the SI distribution. We applied the framework to synthetic exposure-history data from epidemics simulated on dynamic contact networks of 166,034 individuals, matching the 2024 population of Oxford, UK. It produced estimates comparable to those from centralised analysis, identified the timing of peak host infectiousness relative to symptom onset to within one day, and reconstructed SI distributions that closely tracked the ground truth. We also systematically assessed how participation levels (app adoption and case ascertainment), technical limitations (incomplete exposure logging), and surveillance (knowledge of the background hazard from unobserved exposures) affected inference, and showed that daily population-level knowledge of the background hazard was sufficient for reliable inference. Implications of all the available evidenceBeyond their role as a control measure, DCT apps could provide timely, population-representative estimates of key transmission parameters, such as the host infectiousness profile and SI distribution. Our findings show that such inference is feasible within the privacy-preserving architectures likely to underpin future DCT systems. Greater app adoption, case ascertainment, and exposure logging would improve inference accuracy. To realise this potential, the framework will need to be embedded in DCT systems, supported by concurrent epidemiological research, real-world validation, and early collaboration with public health authorities and platform providers.

papers.title: The role of personality traits in COVID-19 vaccination: A socio-cultural and gender-stratified analysis in Japan
papers.abstract: BackgroundCOVID-19 vaccination uptake is influenced by various sociodemographic and psychological factors. Previous studies have suggested that the relationship between personality traits and vaccination is context-dependent. However, this association has not been investigated in Japan--a unique sociocultural context characterized by historically low vaccine confidence but exceptionally high COVID-19 vaccine uptake. We examined the association between the Big Five personality traits and completion of the primary COVID-19 vaccination series, exploring potential gender-personality interactions. MethodsA web-based, cross-sectional survey was conducted among 7,210 Japanese adults (aged 20-85 years) in December 2021. Personality was assessed using the Japanese version of the Ten-Item Personality Inventory. Multivariable Poisson generalized estimating equations were used to calculate adjusted prevalence ratios (PRs) and assess gender-personality interactions. ResultsHigher extraversion and lower openness were significantly associated with vaccination completion across genders. A significant gender-agreeableness interaction was observed: agreeableness (PR = 1.016, 95% CI: 1.008-1.024) was positively associated with vaccination completion among men but not women. A similar, though only marginally significant, interaction pattern was observed for neuroticism (PR = 1.011, 95% CI: 1.004-1.019 among men). ConclusionsPersonality traits act as modest but meaningful, gender-specific psychological modifiers of vaccination behavior in Japan. Public health campaigns should transition from traditional "one-size-fits-all" messages to personality-tailored and gender-responsive communication strategies to optimize vaccine uptake and bolster psychological resilience in future pandemics.

papers.title: Rates of oral nicotine pouch experimentation, initiation, and cessation by other tobacco product use and sociodemographic characteristics among U.S. adults, 2022-2024
papers.abstract: ImportanceOral nicotine pouches (ONPs) are tobacco-leaf-free nicotine products that have experienced a substantial increase in sales in recent years. ObjectiveTo determine how ONP experimentation, initiation, and cessation rates differ by other tobacco product use and sociodemographic characteristics. DesignNationally representative longitudinal cohort study; data from Waves 7 and 8 (2022-2024) of the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health (PATH) Study. SettingUS civilian, non-institutionalized population. ParticipantsAdults in Waves 7 and 8 of PATH. Of 27,800 eligible participants, 24,640 with complete information on the exposure and outcome were included. ExposuresOther tobacco product use (cigarette-only, electronic nicotine delivery system [ENDS]-only, smokeless tobacco [SLT]-only, and multiproduct use) and sociodemographic characteristics (sex, race and ethnicity, age, and educational attainment). Main OutcomesHazard rates and ratios of transitioning between never, current, and non-current ONP use, defined by ever and past-30-day use, overall and by exposure group. Rates are estimated in univariable weighted multistate transition models. ResultsAmong 24,640 participants, 23,555 (96.7%) never used, 802 (2.5%) non-currently used, and 283 (0.8%) currently used ONPs in 2022. From 2022-24, ONP initiation was higher among those using cigarettes only (HR 3.34, 95% CI 1.59-7.02), ENDS only (HR 9.68, 95% CI 2.89-32.5), SLT only (42.4, 95% CI 22.3-80.7), or multiple products (HR 18.4, 95% CI 7.11-47.8) compared to those who did not use these tobacco products. Those who used cigarettes only (HR 3.02, 95% CI 1.24-7.34), ENDS only (HR 2.03, 95% CI 1.11-3.71), or multiple products (HR 2.61, 95% CI 1.12-6.09) discontinued ONPs at higher rates than those using no other products. Men had higher ONP initiation and lower cessation rates than women, adults ages 35+ years had lower initiation rates than those ages 18-24, and non-Hispanic Black participants had higher cessation rates than non-Hispanic White participants. Conclusions and RelevanceInitiation of ONPs was higher among those who used other tobacco products, highlighting the need to investigate whether ONPs replace these products or lead to poly-tobacco use. Higher cessation rates among those using cigarettes only or ENDS only may suggest experimentation rather than sustained use. Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSHow do rates of oral nicotine pouch (ONP) experimentation, initiation, and cessation depend on other tobacco product use and sociodemographic characteristics? FindingsAmong 24,640 adults in a nationally representative longitudinal cohort study, individuals using other tobacco products experimented with and initiated ONPs at higher rates than those not using other tobacco products, but all except those using only smokeless tobacco also discontinued ONPs at higher rates. MeaningAdults using other tobacco products were more likely to experiment with but not necessarily continue to use ONPs in this period in which ONPs were recently introduced.

papers.title: Proteomic markers of colorectal cancer risk: results from the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition
papers.abstract: 1.BackgroundCirculating proteins are promising biomarkers of colorectal cancer risk. Most studies combine colon and rectal cancer despite their biological differences. ObjectiveTo identify proteins associated with colorectal, colon, and rectal cancer risk and triangulate findings using cross-cohort confirmation and Mendelian randomisation (MR). DesignWe profiled 6,402 proteins, using the SomaScan 7K assay in a case-cohort study nested within the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC; 658 colon and 319 rectal cancers). Cox models identified proteins associated with cancer risk at a false discovery rate <5%. Findings were confirmed in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study (ARIC; SomaScan; 235 colon, 36 rectal) and UK Biobank (Olink Explore; 321 colon, 164 rectal). MR and genetic colocalisation evaluated potential causality. ResultsWe identified 36 proteins associated with colorectal cancer, 50 with colon cancer, and 2 with rectal cancer; 20 of the 36 were also associated with colon cancer and none with rectal cancer, and no protein was associated with both sites. Seven of the 40 colon cancer proteins available in ARIC were confirmed, including COMP, MIC-1/GDF15, TFF3, and THIK. Of these, MIC-1/GDF15 and TFF3 were also confirmed in UK Biobank. COMP was inversely associated with colon cancer risk observationally and in MR analyses. ConclusionColon and rectal cancers have different pre-diagnostic proteomic profiles, underlining the need for site-specific analyses. COMP, MIC-1/GDF15, and TFF3 were the most robustly supported biomarkers of colon cancer risk. Future work should prioritise experimental validation of these associations and use of repeated measures to define timing. 2. Key messagesWhat is already known on this topic: Circulating proteins have been linked to colorectal cancer risk, but few have been validated prospectively and most studies have combined colon and rectal cancer despite their recognised biological differences. What this study adds: Colon and rectal cancers had distinct pre-diagnostic proteomic profiles with no overlapping associations, and the colorectal cancer signal was driven almost entirely by colon cancer. COMP, MIC-1/GDF15, and TFF3 were associated with colon cancer risk in EPIC and confirmed in independent cohorts, with genetic support for COMP. How this study might affect research, practice or policy: Proteomic studies of colorectal cancer should be analysed by anatomical site, and COMP, MIC-1/GDF15, and TFF3 warrant experimental validation as markers of colon cancer risk.
